Introduction - August 2010 











##### **Introduction** 

In the July issue of the Base Metals One Year Forecast, we questioned whether the price weakness seen in June represented a buying opportunity.  We commented, “GFMS believes that we may see a repeat of the price patterns seen in late January/early February and then again in April, when the sharp correction in prices was seen by many market participants – consumers, service centres, traders, as well as the financial community – as a buying opportunity rather than as a signal of a b

roader weakness in industrial commodities”. This was certainly the case in July with sharp gains across all the LME-traded metals. The GFMS’ Base Metal Index (BMI) increased by 14% from 248.07 at the beginning of month to a high of 282.78 at the end of July. The BMI made further gains in early August. However, we believe that there will be a retracement as August progresses. ###### **Have prices got ahead of the fundamentals?** A key feature of this price cycle has been prices rallying sharply in anticipation of an improvement in the market fundamentals (January-February and then again in April). The July rally comes into this category as there was not a major shift in the fundamentals, although the market did receive some support from the downtrend in LME stocks. However, many other aspects are less supportive of the recent double-digit rebound in prices. On the supply side, the increase in Chinese mine and refined production continues to gather pace. The increases to Chinese mine output have been particularly strong, which has allowed refined production to expand (see individual sections for details). ###### **Chinese trade data is bearish** Although most data points to still strong growth within China, higher production has tended to outpace demand growth leading to changes in the net trade balance from ###### **~~Base Metals & Other Commodity Prices~~** 250

China. For aluminium, the near 50% increase in production has seen the country turn from being a significant net importer to being a net exporter of metal (including alloys). A similar situation prevails for lead, while for zinc and nickel net imports have fallen sharply. China’s imports of refined nickel have fallen by around 50% this year; however this has been offset by a near doubling of nickel concentrate imports, which have fuelled a rise in nickel pig iron production. Although net imports of refined copper have fallen by around 15%, the decline is relatively small given the inventory overhang that was built up last year. For tin, the situation is somewhat different with the country remaining a net importer of refined metal, which is a reversal of its historic position of being a net supplier to the tin market. ###### **Production growth accelerates** We analyse production trends in detail within the individual sections. However, the combination of high prices and earlier expansions has encouraged higher output. From a bearish perspective, aluminium and zinc stand out in terms of production growth so far this year. At the other extreme reside copper and tin, where structural tightness means that the supply response has been constrained despite the relatively high prices. ###### **Where is next

“batch” of bullish news coming from?** A recurring theme of our analysis is that the market requires a constant stream of bullish to support prices when they move away from the historic relationship between inventories and prices. We believe that this bullish news flow may dry up in the short term. As noted above, GFMS believes that the news flow from China may not be that supportive in the coming months. We also believe that markets will increasingly focus during the remainder of the third quarter on what can only be described as “less than encouraging” economic data. As such, we expect that the GFMS BMI will trend lower during the remainder of August and in the early part of September. ###### **~~Base Metals Prices in Major Currencies~~** 250

Given the sharp increase in base metal demand in the first half, we expect much slower demand growth in the second part of the year. The biggest concern resides with China. In terms of prices there was however, a relatively muted response to the latest Chinese Purchasing Managers’ index (PMI). The country’s manufacturing sector grew at the slowest pace in 17 months in July as the government clamped down on property speculation and investment in energy-intensive and polluting factories. The PMI fell to 51.2 from 52.1 in June. The key indicators that we track are industrial production and fixed asset investment; both indicators have shown slower growth in recent months. The next release will be in the middle of August, GFMS is expecting a further slowdown in the rate of growth. Although a lot of attention has been focused on the correction in the construction sector, we also note that vehicle production has fallen (month-on-month) for the last four months. BYD, the Chinese carmaker, has slashed its sales forecast for this year by 25% as growth in the world’s largest auto market slows. The revision comes amid signs of softening in China’s car market. ogresses. Our favoured indicator, the ISM, fell to 55.5 in July from 56.2 in June. Although the index remains comfortably above the 50 mark (the difference between economic expansion and contraction), the index has now registered three successive declines. The new orders component declined by 5 points to 53.5, its lowest level since June 2009. Manufacturing’s expansion remains intact, but it is certainly losing momentum. The best that can be said about the US auto sector is that (post scrappage deals) sales appear to be stabilising above 11m units on a seasonally adjusted annualised rate basis. US vehicle sales improved in July to 11.5m units, partly due to a specific incentive scheme by Toyota. The lacklustre recovery of the labour market and still-constricted access to credit are weighing on sales. The other key market for US base metals demand – construction – is lagging rather than leading the recovery. Data pertaining to both the residential and non-residential sector continue to point to a slow recovery from this sector. Construction spending rose slightly in June (0.1%) from May, but remains around 8% below year earlier levels. Total construction spending and private construction spending are still near a cyclical low, reflecting both the weak state of the economy and the status of construction spending as a lagging cyclical indicator. An increase in foreclosure rates in the past two months highlights the fragility of the housing market. Private non-residential construction spending is falling and is at its lowest level since 2005. The two key consumer sentiment indicators – The Conference Board and the University of Michigan consumer sentiment index – have both eased in recent months. Independent - Informed - International **E2** Economic Indicators - August 2010 ###### **Will growth in the Euro zone falter?** At the moment, confidence remains high in the Euro zone as the economic sentiment index in July rose to its highest level in two years to 101.3 from a revised 99 in June. However, we believe that this may be the peak given the ongoing concerns over the sustainability of the economic recovery and European sovereign debt problems. The Euro zone recovery will not be helped by the latest bout of dollar weakness. The factors that have supported confidence (and economic growth) – higher exports, restocking, and government fiscal stimulus measures may not feature so prominently in the second half of the year. Moreover, emerging market economies such as China and India, which are beginning to take steps to rein in surging local inflation, will probably contribute rather less to world GDP growth than they have over the past year or so. In light of this, we expect a marked deceleration in global GDP growth later this year or early in 2011, with next year’s GDP growth figure correspondingly now forecast at 2.3%. This is followed by marginally faster growth in 2012 as the more traditional sources of growth, such as consumer spending, start to improve. The latter will be aided by unemployment beginning to slowly recede, albeit from elevated levels. ###### **Rapid Japanese demand growth may come to an end** One feature of base demand so far this year has been the sharp rebound in Japan; however we doubt whether the rate of underlying economic growth will support further gains. Industrial production declined 1.5% month-on-month in June, although it was still 16.9% higher year-on-year. In common with a number of other mature economies, the impact of the earlier stimulus measures is beginning to fade. The strong yen is hitting exports as is the slower growth in both the United States and China. ###### **GFMS economic projections** GFMS has reassessed its economic forecasts. These will be discussed in more detail in our Quarterly Three Year Copper Forecast that will be published later this week. For more details concerning this report contact: Charles. demeester@gfms.co.uk. Our projections for the global economy in 2010 are largely unchanged. Accordingly we now forecast world GDP growth to be 3.0% in 2010, up a fraction from 2.9% in our April forecast. Despite this, our Base Case Scenario has become slightly

gloomier in terms of the outlook for 2011 and 2012 because of the indebted nature of both governments and consumers in much of the developed world. As the artificial stimulus of deficit spending starts to be withdrawn and as monetary policy is also slowly tightened (in response to a pick-up in inflation) GDP growth is likely to slow in both the United States and Europe. **E3** Independent - Informed - International Copper - August 2010 ##### **Copper** ###### **Recent developments** - **_The key supportive drivers of the copper market – tight concentrate supply and strong underlying growth within China remain in place._** - **_Reported inventories have continued to fall in recent weeks. At end-July, LME stocks stood at 413,075 tonnes and have trended marginally lower in early August._** - **_Official Chinese production and trade flows data illustrates a declining apparent consumption against rising semis fabrication, suggesting excess supply in the country may well be on the decline and a near-balanced market is not out of sight._** **_growth in mine output so far this year. GFMS expects that tightness at the concentrate stage will continue to underpin the copper market._** - **_Our supply-demand projections for the next twelve months remain largely unchanged from the previous edition of our Base Metals One Year Forecast and we continue to see the market move into deficit in the final quarter._** - **_Although our Base Case scenario paints a positive scenario for copper prices going forward, we continue to ascribe significant probability to our bearish Scenario C. Linked to deteriorating conditions in European debt markets, further worsening of the economic backdrop in the United States and material slow-down in China, this scenario sees prices trend downwards well into the next year._** ###### **Outlook for the next 12 months** - **_Prices across the base metals complex have rallied in recent weeks. We believe that prices have got ahead of the fundamentals and expect that there will be a correction in the price in the short-term._** - **_Nevertheless many of the drivers behind the recent rise in the copper remain in place. Independent - Informed - International **C1** Copper - August 2010 ###### **Market background** The last couple weeks have once again turned the tables for copper. Fuelled by a series of positive developments on the global economic backdrop, prices rallied, in parallel with other industrial commodities but also equity prices. Although little change was noted on the metals fundamentals or their outlook, investment activity coupled with seasonally thin volumes saw prices rally to the recent peak of $7,420/tonne in early August, up 16.8% from the levels noted at the beginning of July and 21.8% compared to this year’s low in early June. As we had iterated on numerous occasions in our recent monthlies, a recovery in copper prices following their collapse to the low-$6,000s was due. This expectation had been based on GFMS’ view, that investors had been overly averse to risk from the eruption of the Greek sovereign credit crisis onwards and that they had tended to overreact to even marginally negative developments in global markets. Specifically, although we believe that copper’s fundamentals are relatively benign, there remain a few more hurdles to overcome before prices in the mid-$7,000s can be justified on a sustainable basis. As such, although we continue to see prices generally trend upwards over the rest of the year, we would expect a correction is likely to occur during the summer months. Likely triggers for such a move are likely to come from disappointing developments on key markets, which, as we note in the introductory section, we are not convinced are behind us quite yet. month at just over 413,000 tonnes, down 36,000 tonnes on their end-July level and nearly 90,000 tonnes lower than at end-2009. Inventories in early August remain around this level. Stocks held at Shanghai Futures Exchange (SHFE) registered warehouses also fell over the course of July, by more than 19,000 tonnes, to less than 105,000 tonnes, the lowest level since early February. ###### **The Chinese market is getting tighter** In previous editions of our Base Metals One Year Forecast, we contended that the copper market had been in surplus over the first six months of the year and that excess supply had likely found its way into Chinese unreported inventories. More recently, we

had noted signs that, although probably still in surplus, the Chinese market was becoming tighter, as semis production rose faster than apparent and reported (i.e. including changes in reported stocks) consumption and scrap availability did not seem to increase sufficiently to offset this. The latest official data to come out of the country continues to support this view. In June, the gap between semis production, which stood at a little less than 942,000 tonnes, and reported consumption, at 648,000 tonnes, stood at around 294,000 tonnes. Against this, net official scrap imports, at a little over 353,000 tonnes, were far off previous highs. Illustrative of the tightening conditions in China are also the quarterly figures, with the cumulative difference between semis production and reported consumption reaching 715,000 tonnes in the second quarter of the year, compared to 262,000 tonnes in the first three months of 2010 and 384,000 tonnes in the second quarter of last year. ###### **Inventories continue to fall** Nevertheless, the declining level of reported stocks of refined copper continues to create a positive backdrop for copper prices, particularly against growing signs that the Chinese market (where the bulk of oversupply this year-todate seems to have been accumulated) is getting tighter. July saw LME inventories continue to decline, ending the Given the above, it looks increasingly likely that the Chinese market is now more or less balanced and the stockpiling, that was particularly pronounced last year but persisted to a lesser extent during the first half of 2010, may now be over. **C2** Independent - Informed - International Copper - August 2010 consideration to the latest revisions of our projected surpluses and deficits, discussed in detail later in this section. ###### **First half production figures confirm production problems** By late July, production figures for some of the largest copper producers had been released. Freeport McMoran reported production of around 850,000 tonnes over the period, down 11% compared to 2009. The company said that it expected to produce a total 1.7 million tonnes of copper this year overall. BHP Billiton’s global production was also down, by 12% year-on-year, during the first half of 2010, totalling approximately 520,000 tonnes. It is also worth noting that in its latest results, BHP also stated it expected production at it

s vast Escondida mine to drop by 5-10% in the 2011 financial year. Finally, Xstrata’s copper mine production suffered a more limited decline of 3%, to reach 434,000 tonnes over the first six months of the year. ###### **Chilean output registers a modest increase** In Chile, the world’s biggest copper producing country, output over the first half of the year totalled 2.2 million tonnes, marking a 1.3% increase compared to the year prior. Looking at June in particular, production rose on a monthon-month basis compared to May, but this was primarily due to the low base in the latter month, the result of industrial action at Collahuasi, as discussed in the previous edition of our One Year Forecast. On a year-on-year basis, production was down by a marginal 0.6% in June, amounting to approximately 465,000 tonnes. The latest official data from China also show mine output growth in the country. In June, production stood at a little over 102,000 tonnes, 5% up on May and 14% up year-on-year. Overall, production over the first half of the year totalled 520,000 tonnes, marking a 25% increase compared to 2009. This, as well as higher imports of copper concentrates and scrap, provided the fuel for the 18% rise in refined production, that stood at 2.3 million tonnes over the period. At end-July, the governor of Zambia’s central bank said that as a result of ongoing mining investments in the country, it expects production will reach 750,000 tonnes in 2010. The bank also stated it expected production to top 1 million tonnes in 2012, boosted, among others, by the development of the Kondola Deep project, owned by Konkola Copper Mines, a subsidiary of Vedanta. Although the former expectation is broadly in line with GFMS’ projections of Zambian mine output, the latter seems optimistic. ###### **LME launches Singapore listed copper contract** In late July, the LME and the Singapore Exchange announced their plan to launch copper (as well as zinc) futures contracts listed on the latter exchange during the first quarter of next year, with plans to launch futures on other metals going forward. The LME also said it considered launching warehousing in Taiwan. ###### **Market outlook** Although we had expected a recovery from the low to mid-$6,000s, where prices stood at around the time of the release of our previous monthly, the speed as well as, more importantly, the extent of the rebound has exceeded expectations. As we discussed earlier in this section, this has in part been a reflection of the persistently high investment interest in base metals markets but also in part due to thin volumes. Elsewhere, the buoyancy that has underpinned copper (and also other base metals as well as equity) prices is based on what we would argue is an excessively optimistic assessment of the positive developments the global macroeconomic backdrop has enjoyed over the last few weeks. Independent - Informed - International **N1** Nickel & Cobalt - August 2010 ###### **Market background** After having fallen to a low of $17,955/tonne on June 8th – for the first time since mid-February – in part reflecting the correction from the over-bought situation seen earlier in the second quarter, the market has rallied strongly to peak at close to $22,100/tonne in early August. The market has been supported by the downtrend in LME inventories and, up until recently, fairly positive economic data. However as the nickel market enters the “summer slowdown”, some of the supportive factors behind the nickel market are being removed. As discussed in the Executive Summary, the economic environment is becoming more uncertain, stainless steel prices remain under pressure and Vale’s Sudbury operations are now back on-stream after the prolonged strike. LME stocks which continued to trend lower since the release of our last Base Metals One Year Forecast, touching an almost 11-month low of 115,950 tonnes on July 26th, saw a reversal subsequent to this date. Inventories have increased by 1,870 tonnes since then to just below 118,000 tonnes as the summer slowdown takes effect. ###### **European stainless prices come under pressure…** In our last report, we said “The likelihood of further reductions in the surcharge in the summer months has also put base prices for stainless steel under pressure.” This trend has indeed continued. Base prices for stainless flat products have been falling on uncertain demand conditions and stockholders are trying to liquidate stock reflecting the earlier weakness in nickel prices. In Europe, for example, the average base prices for 304 2mm cold roll sheet fell to €1,100-1,200/tonne ex-works, down from €1,200-1,300/tonne at the start of July. The alloy surcharge for the same product, currently at €1,6001,700/tonne is also expected to fall by about €100-200/ tonne on volatile nickel prices. However, in the case of Europe, it should be noted that the situation in south is far worse than that in north. Orders for September are reportedly poor as stockholders and key c

onsumers are staying on the sidelines where possible. ###### **…however market revival is expected in the fourth quarter** According to its latest interim report, Outokumpu expects the market for its standard grade product to revive in the fourth quarter, after a seasonal dip in the third quarter. Importantly, the company expects orders to start flowing in within the next 6-12 months. In terms of its results, the company saw its deliveries increase only slightly over the second quarter to 339,000 tonnes, despite improving end-user demand. Deliveries are expected to be 10-20% lower in the current quarter as the company’s facilities begin summer maintenance and seasonal factors restrict demand in Europe. Acerinox has also recently released its results for the first half of the year. Over this period, melting production amounted to 1.1 million tonnes, 41% higher than in the first half of 2009. In the second quarter, this figure came in at 559,200 tonnes, however, just 4.4% up on the first quarter. The company closed the first half of the year with increasing capacity utilisation rates, mainly benefitting from the recovery of the North American market. Nevertheless, Acerinox has also been noting slower activity in the current quarter, but believes market conditions will improve once the summer months come to an end. ###### **Asian stainless prices are picking up** China’s largest stainless producer, Shanxi Taigang, recently raised its 304 grade domestic stainless list prices by $74/ tonne after keeping them unchanged for almost the past two months. 3-12mm hot rolled coil rose to $3,145/tonne while, 2B 2mm cold rolled coil increased to $3,263/tonne. The problem for cobalt producers is that inventories in the key Chinese market are relatively high. Demand from the battery manufacturers has been affected by government initiatives to clamp down on the “fake branded” mobile phone sector. Anecdotal evidence suggests that battery orders at a leading manufacturer have fallen by over 70% year -on-year in July. Other reports suggest that this downturn is widespread with July orders some 30% below first half levels. Another problem for cobalt suppliers is the high level of stocks within the country. On the supply side, we are seeing higher production from the African copper-cobalt belt. According to the Bank of Zambia, the country produced 4,057 tonnes of cobalt in the first half of this year, up from 1,967 tonnes in the corresponding period of 2009. Output in June was at a high for the year. Exports of cobalt in this period were 3,889 tonnes up from 1,950 tonnes a year earlier. Eurasian Natural Resources Corp (ENRC) has reported that cobalt output in the second quarter at its Chambishi smelter (acquired in February 2010) was 965 tonnes. KLK Jiangsu Cobalt Nickel Metal Co., the Chinese producer, plans to raise output by 66% in the year to March 2011 to 2,000 tpy from 1,200 tonnes.
